Summary: The paper builds a benchmark for writing OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited (100 entries with 2-12 references; 515 papers, 19% readable in full via open access; causal gene withheld) and compares generation strategies with the model (Claude Opus 5.5), guards, a claim-level citation audit with one repair round, and the scoring held fixed. The strategies are direct reading of all papers in one prompt, an agentic curator, an evidence graph, a per-patient case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, three add-ons (second-hand passages, a reconciled case database, a learned guide) and four 'reading better' arms run on held-out entries. The primary endpoint scores what a draft says about each cited paper against 6,652 facts split once, without sight of any draft, from OMIM's allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar. Results: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries; Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 22); the reading strategies convey 91.0-94.4% of facts the supplied text is judged to state and 5.5-6.9% of the rest (Fig. 2c, Table 18); the agent and the evidence graph are not distinguishable from direct reading and the case table trails by 1.9 points (Table 1); a completeness pass adds 2.6 points (95% CI 1.7 to 3.6) on 38 held-out entries without lowering judged support (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 3b, Table 30); released PaperQA2 and GraphRAG convey fewer facts on 10 and 4 entries and STORM produced no output (Sec. 4.4); and planted errors show that the best-verdict audit catches citation swaps and single-value substitutions but not added citations or omissions (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4). All three reviewers score the paper 5/10 with confidence 4 and recommend rejection. They agree that the controlled design, the fixed fact lists, the symmetric handling of completion and the audit stress test are careful and useful. They also agree on the main problems: every judgement (fact splitting, coverage, 'stated', audit) is made by the writer's own model family and none is validated by a person; the headline access effect is expected by construction; the near-null comparison between strategies is measured in a regime that favours direct reading and moves with implementation settings (App. F); only one proprietary model is tested; and the presentation is very dense.
Strengths: Controlled design: the model, guards, audit and scoring are fixed and only the strategy varies; the papers are fixed to the curators' own reference list, and access is manipulated within papers, which separates what was read from how it was read (Sec. 3, Fig. 1). The reviewers know of no comparison of long-context, graph, agentic and extraction designs that holds this much fixed for knowledge-base writing against curator text.

The within-paper access manipulation is a clean causal design: the full text of the same 91 papers is hidden and each entry rewritten from abstracts, with and without second-hand passages, compared like for like with no arm repaired (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 22). The stated/not-stated split of every fixed fact (Fig. 2b-c, Table 18) is a useful diagnostic that locates the remaining headroom mostly in access.

Measurement hygiene is careful and reusable. Fact lists are fixed once before any draft is seen, and the paper shows that splitting afresh per draft inflates levels by 2-5 points (Table 5). Completion is treated symmetrically, with an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 10) and an explicit account of why stops cost one-call strategies whole entries but per-paper strategies single papers (Sec. 3.3, Table 4). An earlier asymmetric analysis that put the evidence graph 2.1 points behind is reported as corrected (Sec. 4.2, App. M.4).

Statistical reporting is restrained: paired per-entry differences with percentile bootstrap intervals, entries better/worse/tied, exact sign tests, Holm adjustment on the secondary measures, and an explicit statement that non-significant differences are not an equivalence claim (Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4.2, Table 7). Judge variation and run-to-run replicate noise are measured and kept separate from the inferential test (App. E, Table 19).

The audit stress test exposes a concrete, general flaw in claim-level citation audits: because a claim takes the best verdict over its cited papers, none of 30 added irrelevant citations was flagged although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for all 176 claims attributed to it; omissions are invisible by construction; and 4-7% of (claim, cited paper) pairs in real multi-citation paragraphs are judged unsupported (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4, Tables 47-50).

The reading-better experiment is the cleanest positive result: prompts were written on three training entries and frozen before 41 held-out entries were run, with Holm adjustment across arms; the gain is located on facts the text states, mostly in full-text papers (Fig. 3b), and fidelity is checked on 20 audited entries (Sec. 4.3, Table 30).

Claims are scoped and reported candidly: negative results (learned guide, reconciliation), deviations, exploratory status of the 4-10-entry experiments, confounds (creation era, development on evaluation entries) and losses to safety-filter stops are stated, with a ledger of every experiment and its entry set (Table 2). A memory-only control read by creation date and a set of 2026 entries address contamination (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 5, App. M.2). The harness and the per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores are released.
Weaknesses: No judgement is validated by a person, and one model family writes, extracts, splits the reference into facts, judges each fact present/partly/absent/contradicted, judges whether the supplied text states each fact, and audits the claims (Sec. 3.2-3.3, Limitation (i)). The 95.7% agreement between two judgings and the judge-variation figures (App. E, Table 19) show self-consistency, not validity, and self-preference (Panickssery et al., 2024, cited in Sec. 2) could shift absolute levels, the stated/not-stated split and the audit's apparent sensitivity. Every headline number (79.8% vs 36.1%, 91-94% of stated facts, the null strategy differences, the 2.6-point completeness gain) rests on these judgements. All reviewers regard a small expert-annotated sample with chance-corrected agreement, or at least a cross-family judge on the 30-entry replicate subset, as the missing piece.

The 91-94% vs under-7% contrast (Fig. 2c, Table 18) conditions coverage on a same-family judgement that the text 'states' a fact, which requires a verified quote (Sec. 3.3). Facts the model can quote are plausibly the ones a reader of that text conveys, and facts needing inference or paraphrase are more likely to be classed as not stated, so part of the contrast may be mechanical or reflect shared judgement tendencies. The paper notes the caveat (Sec. 4.1), but this contrast is presented as half of the evidence that access bounds agreement; the hidden-full-text experiment (Fig. 2a) is the clean evidence.

The primary comparison does not match settings across paradigms: writers run at high reasoning effort, per-paper extraction in the evidence graph and case table at medium effort, and their synopsis terms are computed by rule (Sec. 3.2, App. B). In the matched ablation the case table moves from -2.3 to -0.2 points and the matched evidence graph is above direct reading (+1.8, +0.4 to +3.3; Sec. 4.2, App. F, Table 21), with sign reversals across entry groups (-1.2 vs +3.1). The paper's own lesson is to 'match settings unrelated to the representation before blaming it' (Sec. 5), yet the unmatched configuration is the headline comparison, and statements such as 'No other design conveyed more than direct reading' (Sec. 1) and 'The designs tested did not beat direct reading' (Sec. 6) are not consistent with the matched result.

The tested regime favours direct reading and leaves little room for strategies to differ: 2-12 references, median input about 39k characters (Sec. 4.4), 81% of papers abstract or title only, 95.5-97.1% coverage already on facts stated in abstract-only papers (Table 18), and about 43% of fixed facts not stated in any supplied text. Between-strategy differences are effectively measured on about 40 entries with stated full-text facts (Fig. 3a). The regime where intermediate representations or agents might separate, many relevant papers, has no comparison: 0 of 4 large entries completed (Sec. 4.4, App. K.2), padding used unrelated papers no draft cited, and the Sec. 5 argument about resolution is 'an observation, not a test'.

The reference is narrow and indirect: OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar, not the narrative sections of phenotype entries (Sec. 3.1). Only about 24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart (App. H, Limitation (ii)), so most generated content is checked only by the unvalidated self-audit, and phenotype or clinical content earns no credit; the title's 'knowledge-base writing' framing claims more than the endpoint measures. Reusability is also unclear: released score files carry fact identifiers, not wording (Ethics statement), and re-splitting shifts levels by 2-5 points (Table 5), so a new strategy may not be scorable against the same 6,652 facts.

Inference and selection are fragile. The case-table deficit (-1.9, -3.1 to -0.8) does not reach p < 0.05 on the sign test (p = 0.071), the primary endpoint is not adjusted across the five comparisons, and under intention to treat it is -1.4 (-4.2 to +1.4) (Sec. 4.2, Table 10); the 'stronger evidence' of -8.4 points on facts stated in full-text papers (40 entries) is not stated to be pre-specified, and many subgroup, era and access-group analyses are reported alongside. The comparison set is selected by non-random safety-filter stops whose reasons are not visible and which are not characterised by topic (7 of 100 main entries, 10 of 30 entries from 2026, all 4 large entries, every STORM entry; Table 2, Table 4), and the two completeness arms lost 3 and 6 of 41 entries while the baseline lost none, with no intention-to-treat result for those arms (Sec. 4.3, Table 27).

The main strategies were developed on the 100 entries they are evaluated on (Limitation (vi)), which may favour the most-iterated prompt; the held-out checks are small (20 compared 2026 entries, App. M.2; 38 entries for reading better). Memorisation remains a live confound for the reading results: memory alone conveys 24.1% of facts in the 600000-609999 band, direct reading's pooled coverage of abstract-only papers falls from 49.8% to 37.9% across creation eras (Sec. 4.2, Tables 14-15), the 1.7% 'in no supplied text' estimate rests on the same judge (Sec. 4.1, Table 17), and the memory-only control already reaches 83.9% causal-gene F1 from the header (Table 1).

Only one proprietary model is evaluated, through an interface with no temperature or seed control and one run per entry (Sec. 3.2, Reproducibility statement). No second model family is tested as writer or as judge, so it is unknown whether the strategy ordering, the near-null differences or the access effect transfer, in particular to weaker or smaller-context models where extraction-first designs are usually motivated; the same model's safety filter also determined which entries and systems could be compared at all.

The released-pipeline comparison is not like for like and is too small for the place it has among the introduction's results (Sec. 1, Sec. 4.4, App. J, Table 32): PaperQA2 ran without its agent, GraphRAG on 4 entries with one small local embedding model, both QA systems answered six fixed section questions whose answers were concatenated, only the authors' drafts went through repair, STORM produced nothing, and n = 10, 4 and 0. It supports little beyond 'not outperformed at these settings'.

The audit stress test is small and partly easy: each qualifier-deletion rule has 2-8 items, swaps are mostly between papers on different topics, all planted errors sit in evidence-graph paragraphs the audit had already passed, and the controls are paragraphs that had passed once (Fig. 4, Tables 47-48). The best-verdict flaw is diagnosed but no per-paper aggregation rule is evaluated for its false-flag cost.

Novelty and significance for ICLR are modest. The strategies are standard instances of known paradigms (long-context reading, GraphRAG-style graphs, agents, self-verification, prompt optimisation), and the reading-better interventions are prompt-level additions. The headline 'access bounds agreement' is expected, as the paper itself says (Sec. 1), and its evidence measures the size of an obvious effect; recall-then-verify may add nothing from the papers, so its 14.6% is largely by construction (Sec. 4.2) and it adds little to the breadth of the comparison. The contribution is mainly a careful domain benchmark, which two reviewers suggest might fit a datasets-and-benchmarks or biomedical-informatics venue better.

Presentation is very dense. Nearly every sentence of Sec. 4 carries several estimates, intervals, entry counts and caveats (e.g., Sec. 4.1 'Second-hand passages', Sec. 4.4 'Input size'); key definitions (pooled vs mean over entries, 'stated', 'partly present', completion, repaired vs unrepaired arms) are scattered across Sec. 3.3 and the appendix; exploratory 4-10-entry runs are interleaved with primary results; design facts such as the reasoning-effort mismatch appear only in App. B and F; the appendix has 52 tables; and the title runs four lines. Primary, pre-specified analyses are hard to separate from secondary and post hoc ones, and noticeable patterns go undiscussed, e.g., direct reading's 34.9% in the classic band against 51-54% elsewhere (Table 15).
Questions: Can domain experts (clinical geneticists or curators) re-judge a stratified random sample of a few hundred items: fact splits against the curator paragraph, present/partly/absent/contradicted statuses, 'stated' judgements and audit verdicts, with chance-corrected agreement and confusion matrices per strategy? Do the orderings in Table 1 and Fig. 3a and the Fig. 2c contrast hold under the human labels?

Can a judge from a different model family (ideally open-weights) re-score the 30-entry replicate subset, and can direct reading and the evidence graph be run with a second writer family, to test self-preference, correlated errors between the 'stated' and 'conveyed' judges, and whether the strategy ordering and the access effect transfer?

How often does the 'stated' judgement mark as not stated a fact that is inferable from the text but not quotable verbatim? A manual check of 50-100 'not stated' facts from full-text papers would show how much of the Fig. 2c contrast is mechanical.

Why does the primary comparison run per-paper extraction at medium effort and assign synopsis terms by rule while writers run at high effort? Given App. F, would you report the matched configuration as the main comparison, ideally on all 93 entries, and revise the statements in Sec. 1 and Sec. 6 accordingly?

Which analyses were pre-specified, in particular the stated/not-stated split and the restriction to facts stated in full-text papers behind the -8.4-point case-table result? If they were not, can the -1.9-point result be reported as the confirmatory test and the restrictions as exploratory?

What are the reading-better results under intention to treat, with a stopped entry scored as zero or falling back to the baseline draft, given that the completeness arms lost 3 and 6 of 41 entries and the baseline none?
How is 'partly present' operationalised, and how do the paired differences change under full-credit-only scoring for each restriction in Table 18 (Table 5 gives 'fully' coverage only for all facts)?

Which entries and papers trigger the safety-filter stops? Are they concentrated in particular disease areas (e.g., reproductive, oncologic or paediatric topics) or in particular strategies' prompts, and how does that affect the 93-entry comparison set and the large-entry experiment?

How many prompt iterations were the main strategies developed through on the evaluation entries, and was any strategy tuned more than another? Could the main comparison be rerun on a fresh held-out sample, and the hidden-full-text comparison reported separately for the newest band or the 2026 entries to bound the role of memory in the 36.1%?
How much does the entry header reveal the withheld causal gene, given that the memory-only control reaches 83.9% gene F1 (Table 1)?

Is there a feasible test of the many-relevant-papers regime (large entries scored only on the subset of references covered by curator paragraphs, reference sets assembled from relevant open-access papers, or a deployment with fewer stops), so that the claim that designs do not separate is tested where they are expected to?
For the released pipelines, would running direct reading through the same six-question protocol make the comparison like for like?

Will the text of the fixed fact lists be released or be deterministically reconstructable from public data, so that a new strategy can be scored against exactly the same 6,652 facts? If reconstruction requires re-splitting with a model, how stable are the resulting lists?

What kinds of facts account for the case table's -8.4-point deficit on stated full-text facts (e.g., functional assays, segregation or population data that are not per-patient records)? Is it a property of the representation or of the extraction schema?

What fraction of the curator facts not stated in full-text papers is likely in supplementary material, and could supplements of the 96 full-text papers be retrieved for the hidden-full-text experiment to bound how much of the access effect is supplement-only content?

Has a per-paper verdict aggregation rule (flag a claim when any cited paper is judged unsupported) been evaluated, and what is its false-flag rate on the real multi-citation paragraphs where 4-7% of (claim, paper) pairs are already judged unsupported?
Why is direct reading's coverage so much lower in the classic 1xxxxx-5xxxxx band (34.9%, Table 15): access, older text, or a property of older OMIM variant paragraphs?
Limitations: The authors list the main limitations candidly and thoroughly (Sec. 5, (i)-(xi)), and the ethics statement addresses clinical misuse and the rights in curated text.

The absence of any human validation is presented as a caveat but limits whether the benchmark can serve others as a reference; it should be addressed, at least on a sample, rather than only acknowledged.

One proprietary model wrote and judged everything, and its safety filter determined which entries and systems could be compared; this should be stated as a limit on the generality of the central 'access over strategy' conclusion, not only as a completion issue.

The unmatched reasoning-effort and synopsis configuration of the main comparison, and the reliance on one implementation per paradigm, should be listed as limitations of the headline between-strategy result (App. F shows settings move the case table by about 2 points).

The regime (few references, mostly abstracts, about 43% of facts not stated in any supplied text) compresses measurable differences between strategies and should be stated as a reason the near-null result may not generalise, beyond the note on large entries.
Not sufficiently addressed: the possible circularity of conditioning coverage on a same-model 'stated' judgement that requires a verbatim quote.
Not sufficiently addressed: selection bias from non-random, uninspectable safety-filter stops, including whether stopped content is topic-related.

Not sufficiently addressed: leakage of the withheld causal gene through entry headers and memorisation of OMIM content, which affect absolute levels on the secondary measures and the provenance analysis.

Licensing and reuse: the reference relies on OMIM text deposited in ClinVar that is not redistributed; whether others can rebuild and score against the same fact lists under the rights holders' terms should be stated explicitly.

Societal: the drafts concern clinical genetics; the paper rightly states they are not clinical guidance and must not be presented as OMIM content. Users should also be warned that a fidelity audit passes a draft that faithfully copies a source's error and does not detect omissions.
